title: Harm categories and severities
summary: Azure AI Content Safety classifies text and images into four harm categories with severity levels. A guardrail control compares the severity to a threshold you choose, so the threshold is your false-positive dial.
useIf: You need a managed first line of defence for hate, sexual, violence and self-harm content in prompts and completions.
avoidIf: Your risk is a custom policy (for example investment advice) or prompt injection: these categories do not cover them.

explain.md: The four categories are **hate and fairness, sexual, violence and self-harm**, for text and images [[r6]]. In Foundry guardrails each category has four severity levels. **Safe** is annotated but never filtered and is not configurable. **Low** is mild material (prejudiced views, mild depictions in fictional contexts, personal experiences). **Medium** is moderate (graphic depictions, bullying, content promoting harmful acts). **High** is severe (extremist content, explicit depictions, content endorsing serious harm) [[r6]].

explain.md: New model deployments get the default guardrail `Microsoft.DefaultV2`: hate, violence, sexual and self-harm at Medium on prompts and completions, plus other controls. It applies to all Foundry Models sold by Azure except audio transcription models. A request over a threshold is blocked with an error that names the category [[r2]]. The standalone service returns a 0 to 7 scale for text, or on request the trimmed scale 0, 2, 4, 6, where each pair maps to one level ([0,1] to 0, [2,3] to 2, [4,5] to 4, [6,7] to 6). The image model returns only 0, 2, 4 and 6 [[r6]].

explain.title: Read the behaviour column, not the adjectives
explain.md: The documentation calls Low the least restrictive setting and High the most restrictive, yet Low flags the most content. Decide by what each threshold flags, as in the table above [[r6]].

whereToUse: Consumer chat assistants that must refuse hateful, sexual, violent or self-harm content
Education and youth products where thresholds should be strict
Professional tools where clinical or legal text uses graphic vocabulary and needs looser settings
Image-capable assistants that moderate uploads and generated images
Audit evidence: annotations record category and severity per request

use: Use the default Medium threshold as the starting point and measure
Use Low thresholds where the audience is vulnerable and over-blocking is cheaper than harm
Use High thresholds with extra controls where professional text would be over-blocked
Use annotations to log severities even when you do not block
avoid: Avoid expecting these categories to catch prompt injection, protected text or custom policy
Avoid assuming equal accuracy in every language: eight were trained and tested
Avoid switching a category Off without approval and a replacement control
flips: Audience becomes children: lower thresholds to Low and add human review
Users become verified professionals: raise thresholds for the categories their work involves
Policy is custom (domain rules): add custom controls or an LLM or classifier you evaluate

pitfalls.symptom: A medical assistant blocks legitimate clinical questions
pitfalls.cause: The default Medium threshold flags graphic but professional vocabulary
pitfalls.fix: Raise the threshold for the affected categories for verified users and add other controls

pitfalls.symptom: Non-English users report more wrongful blocks
pitfalls.cause: Detection accuracy and false positive rates can vary outside the eight tested languages
pitfalls.fix: Build a per-language evaluation set and tune per language

pitfalls.symptom: A long prompt is not fully moderated
pitfalls.cause: Documentation mentions moderation of the first 1,000 characters in some scenarios and limits differ by API (wording unclear, UNVERIFIED)
pitfalls.fix: Test with long prompts and chunk inputs yourself

pitfalls.symptom: Team confused about which threshold is stricter
pitfalls.cause: The docs call Low least restrictive although it flags the most
pitfalls.fix: Document thresholds by what they flag

scenarios.title: Homework helper for children
scenarios.situation: A learning assistant is used by children aged 8 to 12 through a school. Parents expect strict filtering. Refusing a harmless question is a minor annoyance.
scenarios.question: How do you set the harm controls?

options.name: Low thresholds on all four categories for input and output, with a human review route
options.why: Low flags the most content, which suits an audience where harm is costly and false positives are cheap.
options.tradeoff: More wrongful blocks and review load.

options.name: Default Medium thresholds plus a topic allow list
options.why: Balanced, with the allow list narrowing scope.
options.tradeoff: Mild but unsuitable content may pass.

options.name: High thresholds to reduce annoyance
options.why: High flags only the most severe content, letting mild material through to children.
options.tradeoff: Right for a professional tool with legitimate graphic content.

flips.then: Return to Medium and measure false positives.
Add per-language tests before trusting thresholds.

scenarios.takeaway: Set thresholds by who is harmed and what over-blocking costs.

scenarios.title: Clinical documentation assistant
scenarios.situation: Clinicians use an assistant to draft notes that discuss self-harm, violence and injury in clinical terms. The default guardrail blocks many legitimate drafts. Users are authenticated staff.
scenarios.question: How do you tune the controls?

options.name: Raise thresholds on the affected categories, annotate and log, and add output review for risky patterns
options.why: It removes wrongful blocks while keeping the most severe content flagged and logged.
options.tradeoff: More misses on moderate content, covered by review.

options.name: Apply for modified guardrails and turn categories Off
options.why: Removes blocking entirely where it is approved.
options.tradeoff: Approval is required and you lose the safety net.

options.name: Keep the default Medium thresholds
options.why: It keeps blocking legitimate clinical text.
options.tradeoff: Right for a public consumer product.

flips.if: The tool opens to the public
flips.then: Return to Medium or Low thresholds.

flips.if: Blocks come from one category only

scenarios.takeaway: Tune per category and audience, and keep logging even when you loosen.

quiz.q: The text model is asked for the trimmed scale (0, 2, 4, 6). A text has a full-scale severity of 5. What trimmed value is returned?
quiz.explain: Each pair maps to one level: [4,5] maps to 4. So severity 5 becomes 4.

quiz.q: Which threshold in a Foundry control flags the most content?
quiz.explain: Low flags severity low and above. High flags only the most severe, Medium sits between and Off disables detection. The docs' adjectives can mislead, so read what each flags.

quiz.q: Which statements about the default guardrail are correct?
options: It sets hate, violence, sexual and self-harm to Medium
It applies to audio transcription models
A request over threshold is blocked with an error naming the category
quiz.explain: The default guardrail uses Medium for the four categories and blocks with a named category. It does not apply to audio transcription models.
